posts:
Some developers spent years reverse-engineering GTA III and Vice City so the games would run properly on modern machines.

The projects shipped no game content. You had to own the original game to use them at all.

Feb 2021: Take-Two files a DMCA notice. GitHub pulls the code.

A counter-notice gets a fork restored. A lawsuit follows that September. The projects come down again in October.

The next month, Take-Two ships its own remasters of both games. The case later settled.

Open the original repo today and GitHub returns:

HTTP 451 — UNAVAILABLE FOR LEGAL REASONS

We checked this morning. A status code invented for censorship, named after Fahrenheit 451, for a rebuild of a 20-year-old game you had to own a copy of to run.

You can argue about who was right. That's not the point.

The point is narrower and harder to dodge: owning the game was never the thing that mattered.

Everyone who bought it bought a LICENCE. The city existed at someone else's discretion.

That is the default condition of every virtual world you have ever entered.

Today we're shipping one that starts from the opposite assumption.

El Dorado is live in beta — a virtual world built on Swop.

https://www.swopme.co/eldorado
You sign in with your swop.id from the Swop app. Not a new game account. Not a new password. The identity you already carry.

On a headset you don't type anything with a controller.

Sign in on your phone, then pair the headset — scan a code via Wallet connections in the Swop app, or enter the short code the headset shows you.

Why this is different in kind, and not just a feature list:

In mainstream games, virtual items are granted under a LIMITED LICENCE. You're not buying property. You're buying permission to use something.

Publishers reserve the right to terminate an account, usually without refund.

A ban doesn't just stop you playing — it freezes the inventory attached to that game.

An inventory you can't reach has no practical value, whatever the market price says.

Most publishers also prohibit transferring items or accounts outside their own systems.

So the exit is controlled by the same party as the entrance.

EVE Online's PLEX is a real exception — but it exists because a publisher chose to allow it, and could choose otherwise.

El Dorado sets that dial differently at the start.

Swop is fully self-custodial: keys are generated and held on your device, and Swop never holds them.

Your access doesn't depend on an account staying in good standing with one operator.

Two more things that follow:

Transactions on Swop are gas-sponsored — no holding SOL or ETH before you can take a first action. Swop absorbs the network fee.

And Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon. Not a per-game balance in one company's ledger.
Lose the phone and you don't lose the account: log in with your email on any phone and your wallet comes back. You can also export your private key and open your assets in another wallet entirely.

Now the part most launch posts skip.

Self-custody is NOT the same as legal ownership.

It changes what can be done to your ACCESS. It doesn't settle what rights you hold in a virtual good — that depends on the terms and your jurisdiction, and the law is genuinely unsettled.

Anyone telling you a wallet converts a game item into property in the legal sense is skipping a step.

We're claiming the custody half, which is real. Not the legal half, which isn't ours to assert.
Also true, and worth weighing before you put anything into a beta: Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date.

And it IS a beta. Literally, not as a legal cushion.

Things will change under you. Some will break. Features will move.

Improvements roll out EVERY WEEK — the version you walk into Monday isn't the one there the Monday after.
Beta is a description, not a disclaimer. It doesn't move the consequences of rough edges onto the people using it. If something behaves badly, that's ours to fix.

Bring a swop.id. If you don't have one, claim it in the Swop app.

https://www.swopme.co/eldorado
